beats.say: Meera asks: can bakery items be refunded after six hours? The answer is sitting in FreshCart's refund policy. Page four. In a table.
Last time we saw the problem. The model never read that page. And we can't paste in all twelve thousand documents.
So think about how you'd answer it yourself. Would you memorise twelve thousand documents?
Of course not. You'd open the right policy, find the right paragraph, read it, and answer. An open-book exam.

That's the whole idea. First, find the few passages that answer the question. Then hand them to the model and say: answer only from these, and show me where. This is called RAG: retrieval augmented generation.
The model stops being the source of facts. It becomes a reader of the evidence you hand it.
Chapter two. Let's build it, one attempt at a time.
Attempt zero: just paste the document.
For one question about one policy, the simplest thing works. Paste the forty-page refund policy into the prompt, add the question, done.
And keep this in your pocket: when your knowledge is small and rarely changes, that's genuinely the right design. No search, no search mistakes.
But agents ask about everything. Refunds, slots, warehouses, franchises. Twelve thousand documents. It will never fit.
Attempt one: search the way you search your own files. Find documents that contain the words of the question.
Ask about error slot expired, and exactly one runbook contains that code. Perfect.
Then an agent types: eggs broken on arrival, can they get money back?
The policy says: damaged items reported within twenty-four hours get a full refund. Look closely. They share almost no words.
Broken versus damaged. Money back versus refund. Keyword search finds nothing. And people will always use different words.
So how can a computer tell that two sentences mean the same thing?
Imagine a map where every sentence has a spot, and sentences that mean similar things live next door.
Refund within twenty-four hours, and money back for damaged items, are neighbours. Delivery slot moved lives in a totally different neighbourhood.
That spot is called an embedding: a list of numbers, the sentence's coordinates in meaning.
Now drop the question on the map. Eggs broken, money back. It lands right next to damaged items, even with no words in common.
Grab whatever is nearest. That's vector search.
The real map has hundreds of directions, not two. But the idea is exactly this.
How does a model learn where to put things? This is the part interviewers love.
Feed it millions of pairs that belong together: a question and its answer. A search and the page people clicked.
Pull each pair together. Push everything else apart. Over and over.
That's called contrastive learning. And the best teachers are look-alike wrong answers, like the bakery rule for a dairy question, because they teach fine differences.
One warning: switch embedding models later, and every document must be embedded again. Different models make different maps.
Now, a trap.
Embed the whole forty-page policy as one spot on the map. Where does it land?
It covers dairy, bakery, frozen food, fees, fraud... so it lands in the blurry middle of everything. A weak match for every question. A sharp match for none.
So cut documents into small cards, one idea each. Each card gets its own sharp spot.
Too big, and it's blurry again. Too small, and you get: the limit is twenty-four hours. The limit on what?
So keep the heading on every card. Refund policy, damaged items, dairy. Now it means something.
What size is right? Don't guess. Try three sizes on real agent questions, and keep the winner. That's the answer interviewers want.
Here's a neat trick to get both: precision and context.
Search the small cards, because small cards are sharp. But when one matches, hand the model its whole section.
Now the model sees the dairy rule, and the photo-proof rule sitting right next to it. This is called parent-child retrieval.
Let's put it all together.
There are two machines, running at different times.
Offline, whenever a document changes: read it, cut it into cards, embed each card, and store them in a vector index.
Online, for every question: embed the question, and grab the twenty nearest cards.
Then a slower, sharper model rereads those twenty and keeps the best five. That's a reranker.
Build the prompt: rules first, the five cards with their labels, the question last.
And the answer cites its sources, so an agent can click and check.
One bug catches almost everyone. The refund policy gets updated to version four.
The team adds the new cards... and forgets to delete the old ones.
Now versions three and four are both searchable, and answers quietly mix them.
Worse: a deleted document stays searchable. That's not a stale answer. That's a data leak. So every update deletes the old version, in the same step.
Last thing. Interviewers rarely ask what RAG is. They ask: why RAG, and not something else?
Missing facts that are large and changing? RAG. Small and fixed? Just put them in the prompt.
Live data, like stock levels? Ask the live system. And: how many refunds did we issue last week?
Search can't count. That's a database query, not RAG.
Let's lock it in.
RAG: find the passages first, then answer only from them.
Keyword search: perfect for exact codes, blind to different words.
Embeddings put meaning on a map, so similar ideas sit close together.
Chunks: one idea per card, with its heading attached.
And a reranker picks the best five from the twenty nearest.
Ask FreshCart goes live. Agents love it. Then, within two weeks, three complaints arrive.
One: it's slow. Every question is compared against two million cards.
Two: the Bengaluru North franchise gets no results at all for its own documents.
Three: error codes fail again. The exact-match power of keyword search got lost.
How would you search two million cards without checking every one? And how do you combine a keyword ranking with a meaning ranking?
That's chapter three. See you there.
